A genuine Rekor v2 entry whose verifier is a certificate — the v3 shape.

Published 2026-08-16 to https://log2025-1.rekor.sigstore.dev (HTTP 201,
logIndex 67673583) and read back out of the log's own static tiles on the
same day. Nothing in this repository authored the log's half of any of it.

  canonicalized_body.json  the Merkle leaf preimage, verbatim, as it came out
                           of the entry bundle at api/v2/tile/entries/x264/349
                           (offset 239, uint16-BE length framing).
  certificate.der          the same certificate, extracted from
                           spec.hashedRekordV002.signature.verifier
                             .x509Certificate.rawBytes.
  checkpoint.txt           api/v2/checkpoint at tree size 67 686 055, with the
                           log's Ed25519 signature and three witness
                           cosignatures (witness.stagemole.eu,
                           witness.navigli.sunlight.geomys.org,
                           staging.witness.transparency.goog).
  inclusion_path.bin       18 audit-path hashes, derived from the log's hash
                           tiles by recomputing complete-subtree hashes — not
                           taken from any server-supplied proof.
  log_index.txt            67673583.

The certificate is exactly the shape §2 specifies: self-signed P-256,
CN "synchronicity zone key", basicConstraints CA:FALSE critical, keyUsage
digitalSignature critical, and one dNSName SAN —
`zone-key-transparency.demo.invalid`. It proves the load-bearing claim the
whole of v3 rests on: **Rekor performs no certificate validation**, so an
apex written into a SAN lands, in the clear, inside the log's Merkle leaf.

What this fixture can prove, and does, in
tests/rekor_zone_key.rs::real_rekor_v3:
  - the leaf is SHA-256(0x00 || canonicalized_body) and the RFC 6962 walk
    over the audit path reaches the checkpoint's root, in a real tree of
    67.7 million entries;
  - the checkpoint verifies under the *embedded* Sigstore log key;
  - the body parses as hashedrekord 0.0.2 with an x509Certificate verifier;
  - the certificate parses, and its single dNSName SAN is the apex;
  - signature.content verifies under the certificate's own key with the
    entry's data.digest as the prehashed message. (Confirmed independently:
    `openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey pub.pem -sigfile sig.der
     -in digest.bin -pkeyopt digest:sha256` → Signature Verified Successfully.
    Because that digest *is* SHA-256(PAE), the same signature verifies as
    ECDSA-SHA256 over the PAE, which is how ring is asked the question.)

What it cannot prove, stated plainly: the in-toto Statement behind the digest
was not preserved by whoever published this demo entry, and a hashedrekord
leaf commits only to the digest — which is precisely why §3's record carries
the Statement bytes alongside the body. So the fixture cannot exercise the
statement-digest, statement-binding or chain checks, and the test asserts
that a full `rekor::verify` over it fails at exactly that step and no
earlier one. The synthetic suite covers the rest, and the DNSSEC chain half
is anchored to reality separately by tests/fixtures/dnssec_chain.
